items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the executive law and the state finance law, in relation to
minority and women-owned business enterprises post completion certification,
duties of the director and creating the minority and women-owned business
enterprise fund
items.lawCode: Add §314-a, amd §§311, 314 & 316, Exec L; add §97-j, St Fin L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S3390

SPONSOR: BAILEY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the executive law and the state finance law, in relation
to minority and women-owned business enterprises post completion certif-
ication, duties of the director and creating the minority and women-
owned business enterprise fund

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to reduce fraud and misuse of the minority
and women-owned business enterprise (MWBE) program.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 requires post completion certifications to be completed, under
penalty of perjury, that the MWBE actually performed the work, performed
the services, or delivered the materials.

Section 2 requires the division of minority and women's business devel-
opment to create an internet registry, and to perform inspections of
MWBEs to weed out fraud and abuse.

Section 3 requires additional regulations to be adopted related to revo-
cations of certifications for felony convictions for fraudulently
misrepresenting the status of an MWBE.

Section 4 permits a court to issue fines double the amount that should
have been paid to an MWBE upon conviction for felony fraud related to
the MWBE program.

Section 5 permits certain fines to be directed to the MWBE fund.

Section 6 establishes the MWBE fund.

Section 7 provides for the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

The Minority-and Women-Owned Business Enterprise (MWBE) program has
served to increase the participation of disadvantaged. individuals in
public contracts, and it has significantly leveled the playing field in
that regard. However, fraud and misuse of MWBEs serves to undercut the
purpose of the program. Each case of MWBE fraud cheats a legitimate
minority- or women-owned business out of a contract.

In November 2014, a New York State Supreme Court Grand Jury issued a
report on the vulnerability of MBE programs to fraud and misuse. The
report revealed significant criminal conduct in the construction indus-
try spanning at least a decade and, within the relatively small sample
of cases reviewed, found evidence that over $10 million äintended for
honest MWBEs had instead gone to fraudulent non-MWBEs.'

In many cases, contractors claimed to use MWBEs to perform Work or
provide the materials required under the contract, but in fact used
businesses that were neither women- nor minority-owned. Contractors also
misrepresented that MWBEs were providing the services or materials, when
the companies that they listed did net have the capacity to do so. In
some instances, invoices and other billing documents were created to
make it appear as though the work and payments flowed to MWBEs, when the
money was merely passed through those businesses to the non-MWBEs that
actually performed the work.

The grand jury report concluded that current laws are not adequate to
prevent MWBE fraud and misuse. This bill, in conjunction with steps
taken at state- and city-level agencies, will serve to deter MWBE fraud
so that legitimate MWBEs are not burdened with additional barriers to
entry.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2017-18: S.3807/A.702(Rodriguez) - Passed Assembly referred to Finance
2019-20: S.2217/A.2670(Rodriguez) - Referred to Finance

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately, provided, however, that the
amendments to article 15-A of the executive law made by sections one,
two, three, and five of this act shall not affect the expiration of such
article and shall be deemed to expire therewith.
